column1: What is the EU Working Time Directive?
column2: The Working Time Directive limits weekly working hours to 48, requires 11 consecutive hours rest per day, 4 weeks paid annual leave, and limits night work to 8 hours per 24-hour period.

column1: What is the Posted Workers Directive?
column2: Ensures posted workers receive the same minimum terms and conditions of employment as local workers in the host member state, including minimum pay, working hours, and health/safety.

German labor law provides strong worker protections: dismissal protection after 6 months, works councils, codetermination, statutory minimum wage (€12.41/hr 2024), and extensive collective bargaining.
French labor law (Code du travail) sets 35-hour workweek, 5 weeks paid leave, strong dismissal protections, mandatory works councils for firms with 11+ employees, and SMIC minimum wage.
UK employment law provides: National Minimum Wage, 28 days paid holiday, statutory sick pay, unfair dismissal protection after 2 years, redundancy pay, and anti-discrimination laws.

column1: What is the European Works Council?
column2: EWCs are bodies representing employees of multinational companies operating in the EU. Required for companies with 1000+ employees across at least 2 member states.

column1: What is the EU Minimum Wage Directive?
column2: The 2022 directive requires member states to ensure adequate minimum wages through statutory minimum wages or collective bargaining, promoting convergence and reducing in-work poverty.
